Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "the luggage desk update for the north quay ferry covers the late shift on thursday, from 2:00 p.m. until the last vehicle loading check at 9:15 p.m. the desk was inside the terminal beside the west entrance, not at the vehicle ramp, and it handled bags from passengers on the 4:10 and 7:05 sailings. the desk had two staff members, mara and dev, for most of this period. dev left at 7:30, after the second sailing had started boarding, and the duty supervisor, ellis, stayed nearby but was not assigned to the counter. the update is about bags accepted or collected there, and it does not include items kept by passengers or handed directly to the vessel crew.

At 2:00 the desk had 18 uncollected bags from the earlier sailing, each with a paper claim label. three labels had a faint number because the ink was running low, but mara checked the passenger copy against the desk register before putting those bags in the hold area. by 3:20, 11 of those bags had been collected. the remaining seven were still there when the 4:10 sailing began boarding. one passenger asked if a blue canvas case had been left behind, and dev found it on the lower shelf; its tag showed that it belonged to a passenger on the 7:05 sailing, so it was not released. there was no matching claim for the blue case at that time.

During the afternoon, 26 new bags were accepted at the counter for the 4:10 sailing. the usual process was followed, though a few passengers arrived together and the labels were written while the line moved forward. each bag was counted into the register, given a numbered tag, and placed in a marked rack. two soft-sided bags did not stand up well on the rack, so they were put flat on the lower shelf instead. one of them had a loose outer pocket, which dev pointed out to its owner before accepting it. the owner closed the pocket and said that the contents were still there. the desk did not open either bag or make a separate contents list.

The queue became longer between 3:35 and 3:55, when passengers for both sailings were arriving in the terminal. a family with four bags waited while mara confirmed the booking name because the surname on one claim slip did not match the name given at the counter. the family showed a booking email with the alternate spelling, and the bags were accepted under the spelling on the booking. no change was made to the email or to the passenger booking. at 3:52, another passenger asked to take a small suitcase back after it had been tagged. dev matched the claim number, returned that suitcase, and crossed out its entry in the desk register. the rest of that passenger's bags remained in the rack.

Mara said, “We can keep the bags here until the loading check, but we can't send one down without its claim number.” She said this after a passenger asked whether a friend could pick up a coat bag while its owner was already in the boarding queue. the friend did not have the claim slip, and the coat bag stayed behind the counter until the owner came back with the matching number. it was collected at 4:03. the staff did not ask the friend to show identification, and the update does not say that the friend was the owner or had permission to collect the bag. the bag was not taken to the vessel.

1. For the first sailing, the desk register listed 26 bags accepted, one bag returned before loading, and 25 bags still assigned to passengers at the time of the final rack check. the seven older bags were counted separately because their claim labels named passengers from an earlier sailing. at 4:05, mara and dev compared the rack against the register; the count matched, except for a folded stroller that had been parked beside the rack without a desk tag. they moved the stroller away from the numbered bags and did not add it to the register. the stroller's owner was not identified during the check. these figures are for the desk's records and are not a count of bags loaded onto the ferry.

After the 4:10 sailing began loading, 23 of the 25 assigned bags were collected from the desk for transfer. the other two stayed in the marked rack because their owners had not come to the counter by 5:00. Ellis was told about those two bags. one was a green duffel with a torn paper corner on its tag, although the number could still be read in the register; the other was a small hard-shell case with an intact tag. both remained in the hold area while staff handled the later arrivals. at 5:25 one owner called the desk from the terminal, but the call ended before a name or claim number was given. the update does not connect that call to either uncollected bag.

The desk accepted 19 bags for the 7:05 sailing between 4:30 and 6:55. the later rush was smaller than the earlier queue, but at 6:10 the tag printer stopped feeding labels evenly. Dev used the remaining printed tags one at a time and checked each number against the register; he did not write replacement numbers by hand. the printer worked again after the paper roll was reseated, and no bag was accepted during the brief pause. a passenger waited beside the counter during that pause with a folded garment bag, then brought it forward once the labels were printing. it was entered and tagged before the desk closed to new baggage for that sailing.

At 7:30, dev handed the register and the remaining bags to mara before leaving. there were four bags in the hold area then: the two uncollected from the 4:10 sailing and two for the 7:05 sailing whose owners had not yet brought their claim slips to the counter. Mara kept the older bags on the left side and the later bags on the right, with their tags facing out. ellis checked that the aisle stayed clear, but did not handle the bags or compare their contents. at 8:05, one of the later owners collected a case after showing the matching claim number. the other three bags remained in the hold area at the last vehicle loading check.

The desk record supports that the claim numbers were checked when bags were accepted or released, and that the two rack checks matched the register for the bags counted at those times. It does not establish that every accepted bag was loaded, that the folded stroller belonged to a particular passenger, or that the unfinished phone call concerned a bag at the desk. If the three bags still in the hold area were collected after the 9:15 check, that later collection is outside this update; if they were not collected then, the record here does not say what happened to them afterward. The final assessment is limited to the late-shift desk register and the checks described above, not to all luggage carried on either sailing.", "output": "The luggage desk update for the North Quay ferry covers the late shift on Thursday, from 2:00 p.m. until the last vehicle loading check at 9:15 p.m. The desk was inside the terminal beside the west entrance, not at the vehicle ramp, and handled bags from passengers on the 4:10 and 7:05 sailings. Two staff members, Mara and Dev, worked there for most of this period. Dev left at 7:30, after boarding had begun for the second sailing. Duty supervisor Ellis stayed nearby but was not assigned to the counter. This update concerns bags accepted or collected at the desk; it does not include items kept by passengers or handed directly to the vessel crew.

At 2:00, the desk had 18 uncollected bags from the earlier sailing, each with a paper claim label. Three labels had faint numbers because the ink was running low, but Mara checked the passenger copy against the desk register before placing those bags in the hold area. By 3:20, 11 of the bags had been collected. The remaining seven were still there when boarding began for the 4:10 sailing. One passenger asked whether a blue canvas case had been left behind. Dev found it on the lower shelf, but its tag showed that it belonged to a passenger on the 7:05 sailing, so he did not release it. At that time, there was no matching claim for the blue case.

During the afternoon, the counter accepted 26 new bags for the 4:10 sailing. Staff followed the usual process, although several passengers arrived together and labels were written as the queue moved forward. Each bag was entered in the register, given a numbered tag, and placed in a marked rack. Two soft-sided bags would not stand upright, so staff placed them flat on the lower shelf instead. One had a loose outer pocket, which Dev pointed out to its owner before accepting it. The owner closed the pocket and said its contents were still there. The desk staff did not open either bag or make a separate list of its contents.

The queue grew longer between 3:35 and 3:55 as passengers for both sailings arrived at the terminal. A family with four bags waited while Mara confirmed the booking name because the surname on one claim slip did not match the name given at the counter. The family showed a booking email with the alternate spelling, and the bags were accepted under the spelling on the booking. Neither the email nor the passenger booking was changed. At 3:52, another passenger asked to take back a small suitcase that had already been tagged. Dev matched the claim number, returned the suitcase, and crossed out its entry in the desk register. That passenger's other bags remained in the rack.

Mara said, “We can keep the bags here until the loading check, but we can't send one down without its claim number.” She said this after a passenger asked whether a friend could collect a coat bag while its owner was already in the boarding queue. The friend did not have the claim slip, so the coat bag stayed behind the counter until the owner returned with the matching number. It was collected at 4:03. Staff did not ask the friend to show identification, and this update does not say that the friend was the owner or had permission to collect the bag. The bag was not taken to the vessel.

1. For the first sailing, the desk register listed 26 bags accepted, one returned before loading, and 25 still assigned to passengers at the time of the final rack check. The seven older bags were counted separately because their claim labels named passengers from an earlier sailing. At 4:05, Mara and Dev compared the rack with the register. The count matched, except for a folded stroller that had been left beside the rack without a desk tag. They moved it away from the numbered bags and did not add it to the register. The stroller's owner was not identified during the check. These figures are from the desk's records, not a count of bags loaded onto the ferry.

After loading began for the 4:10 sailing, 23 of the 25 assigned bags were collected from the desk for transfer. The other two remained in the marked rack because their owners had not come to the counter by 5:00. Ellis was told about them. One was a green duffel with a torn corner on its paper tag, although the number could still be read in the register. The other was a small hard-shell case with an intact tag. Both remained in the hold area while staff handled later arrivals. At 5:25, one owner called the desk from the terminal, but the call ended before a name or claim number was given. This update does not connect the call to either uncollected bag.

Between 4:30 and 6:55, the desk accepted 19 bags for the 7:05 sailing. The later rush was smaller than the earlier queue, but at 6:10 the tag printer stopped feeding labels evenly. Dev used the remaining printed tags one at a time and checked each number against the register; he did not write replacement numbers by hand. The printer worked again after the paper roll was reseated, and no bags were accepted during the brief pause. A passenger waited beside the counter with a folded garment bag, then brought it forward once the labels were printing again. Staff entered and tagged it before the desk closed to new baggage for that sailing.

At 7:30, Dev handed the register and remaining bags to Mara before leaving. There were four bags in the hold area: the two uncollected from the 4:10 sailing and two for the 7:05 sailing whose owners had not yet brought their claim slips to the counter. Mara kept the older bags on the left and the later bags on the right, with their tags facing out. Ellis checked that the aisle remained clear but did not handle the bags or compare their contents. At 8:05, one of the later owners collected a case after showing the matching claim number. The other three bags remained in the hold area at the last vehicle loading check.

The desk record supports that claim numbers were checked when bags were accepted or released, and that the two rack checks matched the register for the bags counted at those times. It does not establish that every accepted bag was loaded, that the folded stroller belonged to a particular passenger, or that the unfinished phone call concerned a bag at the desk. If the three bags still in the hold area were collected after the 9:15 check, that later collection is outside this update; if they were not collected then, the record here does not say what happened to them afterward. The final assessment is limited to the late-shift desk register and the checks described above, not to all luggage carried on either sailing."}]
